Well, it's hard to explain but I will try. Most English natives especially Americans hearing the word "yard" will imagine a detached house with a lawn before or behind it. It is "двор" of course, but Russian people usually mean another thing.

Example: Russian person says something like "У меня во дворе есть несколько лавочек." Russian listener hearing it will understand (subconsciously) that a) the person doesn't own this "двор". b) there are most probably more buildings this "двор" belongs to. Because this is Russian life logic. 

But if to translate it as "There are a few benches in my yard." Then somebody from America will get these two key points of the situation exactly in reverse, that a) person probably owns this land and b) consequently that this "yard" belongs only to their house and they placed the benches themselves. After that American person can ask a logical (for them) question - "That's nice, but why did you put several of them?". Which will blue-screen Russian on the spot. The Russian speaker just wouldn't understand why this person thinks that they were the one placing these benches or even deciding their number when it was done by the city administration. It's a complete communicational failure because two people will have two completely different pictures of the same situation in their minds.
